specStatements.text: Students should be able to describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced.

Monoclonal antibodies are produced from a single clone of cells. The antibodies are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen and so are able to target a specific chemical or specific cells in the body.

They are produced by stimulating mouse lymphocytes to make a particular antibody. The lymphocytes are combined with a particular kind of tumour cell to make a cell called a hybridoma cell. The hybridoma cell can both divide and make the antibody. Single hybridoma cells are cloned to produce many identical cells that all produce the same antibody. A large amount of the antibody can be collected and purified.
Students should be able to describe some of the ways in which monoclonal antibodies can be used.

Some examples include: For diagnosis such as in pregnancy tests.; In laboratories to measure the levels of hormones and other chemicals in blood, or to detect pathogens.; In research to locate or identify specific molecules in a cell or tissue by binding to them with a fluorescent dye.; To treat some diseases: for cancer the monoclonal antibody can be bound to a radioactive substance, a toxic drug or a chemical which stops cells growing and dividing. It delivers the substance to the cancer cells without harming other cells in the body.
Students are not expected to recall any specific tests or treatments but given appropriate information they should be able to explain how they work.
Monoclonal antibodies create more side effects than expected. They are not yet as widely used as everyone hoped when they were first developed.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item asks students to recall a named test, named drug or named disease. The only item set in a treatment context (q03) supplies the appropriate information in the stem - that the antibody is bound to a toxic drug and binds to an antigen found only on the cancer cells - and asks students to explain how that treatment works. The uses named in the concepts (pregnancy tests, measuring hormone levels, detecting pathogens, fluorescent dyes in research, cancer treatment) are only the examples given in the specification itself.

The whole of 4.3.2 is biology only and Higher Tier only, so every concept, misconception and question in this set is tagged tier "higher". Nothing in the set goes beyond the production route stated in the specification - stimulated mouse lymphocytes, combination with a particular kind of tumour cell, hybridoma cell, cloning, collection and purification. No detail of fusion techniques, antibody structure beyond the binding site, or the immune response mechanism from 4.3.1 is introduced.

concepts.definition: An antibody produced from a single clone of cells. Monoclonal antibodies are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen, and so are able to target a specific chemical or specific cells in the body.

The cell made when mouse lymphocytes, which have been stimulated to make a particular antibody, are combined with a particular kind of tumour cell. The hybridoma cell can both divide and make the antibody.

concepts.term: Cloning and purification of the antibody
concepts.definition: Single hybridoma cells are cloned to produce many identical cells that all produce the same antibody. A large amount of the antibody can then be collected and purified.

concepts.term: Monoclonal antibodies in diagnosis and research
concepts.definition: Uses that depend on the antibody binding to one specific antigen: for diagnosis, such as in pregnancy tests; in laboratories to measure the levels of hormones and other chemicals in blood, or to detect pathogens; and in research to locate or identify specific molecules in a cell or tissue by binding to them with a fluorescent dye.

For cancer, the monoclonal antibody can be bound to a radioactive substance, a toxic drug or a chemical which stops cells growing and dividing. It delivers the substance to the cancer cells without harming other cells in the body.

misconceptions.question: In the production of monoclonal antibodies, what does the tumour cell give the hybridoma cell?
misconceptions.correct: The ability to divide, so that many identical cells can be produced from one hybridoma cell.
misconceptions.misconception: The tumour cell is the part that makes the antibody, and the lymphocyte is only there to keep the hybridoma cell alive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate tumour cells with rapid growth and treat them as the active partner, and the word hybridoma sounds like a kind of tumour. The role of the lymphocyte is easily lost because the stimulation step happens before the two cells are combined.
misconceptions.correction: Mouse lymphocytes are stimulated to make a particular antibody, and these lymphocytes are combined with a particular kind of tumour cell. It is the hybridoma cell formed that can both divide and make the antibody.

misconceptions.question: Can one monoclonal antibody be used to detect several different chemicals in a blood sample?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is specific to one binding site on one protein antigen, so it targets only that specific chemical.
misconceptions.misconception: A monoclonal antibody binds to a range of different antigens, so one antibody can be used against many different targets.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Earlier work on the immune response describes antibodies in general terms as attacking pathogens, so students carry over a picture of antibodies as general purpose defence molecules rather than as molecules with one binding site.
misconceptions.correction: Monoclonal antibodies are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen and so are able to target a specific chemical or specific cells in the body.

misconceptions.question: Why are monoclonal antibodies not yet as widely used as everyone hoped when they were first developed?
misconceptions.correct: Because they create more side effects than expected.
misconceptions.misconception: Monoclonal antibodies cause no side effects, because they only bind to the cells they are meant to target.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The statement that the antibody delivers a substance to the cancer cells without harming other cells in the body is generalised into the idea that the treatment cannot harm the patient at all.
misconceptions.correction: Monoclonal antibodies create more side effects than expected. They are not yet as widely used as everyone hoped when they were first developed.

misconceptions.question: How does a monoclonal antibody bound to a toxic drug treat cancer?
misconceptions.correct: It delivers the toxic drug to the cancer cells without harming other cells in the body.
misconceptions.misconception: The monoclonal antibody itself destroys the cancer cell that it binds to, so the substance bound to it is not needed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students carry over from the immune response the idea that antibodies deal with the cells they attach to, so they see binding itself as the killing step rather than as a way of delivering something.
misconceptions.correction: For cancer, the monoclonal antibody can be bound to a radioactive substance, a toxic drug or a chemical which stops cells growing and dividing. It delivers the substance to the cancer cells.

misconceptions.question: Why do all of the antibodies collected from a clone of hybridoma cells bind to the same antigen?
misconceptions.correct: Because single hybridoma cells are cloned to produce many identical cells that all produce the same antibody.
misconceptions.misconception: The cells used are a mixture of different cells, so the antibody that is collected is really a mixture of antibodies with different targets.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Collecting and purifying a large amount of antibody sounds like bulk production from many sources, and students often read monoclonal as meaning many clones rather than one clone.
misconceptions.correction: Monoclonal antibodies are produced from a single clone of cells. Single hybridoma cells are cloned to produce many identical cells that all produce the same antibody, and a large amount of that antibody can be collected and purified.

mcqs.stem: Mouse lymphocytes are stimulated to make a particular antibody. They are then combined with a particular kind of tumour cell. What does the tumour cell allow the hybridoma cell to do?

options.text: Make the antibody that is later collected.
options.rationale: A student who believes the tumour cell is the antibody producing partner picks this. It is wrong because the lymphocyte was stimulated to make the particular antibody; the tumour cell is combined with it so that the hybridoma cell can divide.

options.text: Make a different antibody as it divides.
options.rationale: A student who thinks cloning produces a mixture of antibodies picks this. It is wrong because the many identical cells produced from a single hybridoma cell all produce the same antibody.

options.text: Divide to produce many identical cells.
options.rationale: Correct. The hybridoma cell can both divide and make the antibody, and single hybridoma cells are cloned to produce many identical cells that all produce the same antibody.

options.text: Kill the cells the antibody binds to.
options.rationale: A student who believes the antibody itself destroys the cells it binds to looks for a killing role in production. It is wrong because destroying cancer cells depends on the substance bound to the antibody, and it plays no part in making the hybridoma cell.

mcqs.stem: A monoclonal antibody is collected from a clone of hybridoma cells and used to measure the level of one hormone in blood. Why does it bind only to that hormone?

options.text: It is made by a mixture of many different cells.
options.rationale: A student who thinks the antibody collected is a mixture picks this. It is wrong because monoclonal antibodies are produced from a single clone of cells that all produce the same antibody, and a mixture would not be specific.

options.text: It is specific to one binding site on one antigen.
options.rationale: Correct. Monoclonal antibodies are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen and so are able to target a specific chemical in the body.

options.text: It is made by one particular kind of tumour cell.
options.rationale: A student who believes the tumour cell makes the antibody assumes the tumour cell decides what it binds to. It is wrong because the specificity comes from the antibody having one binding site for one protein antigen.

options.text: It is able to bind any antigen in the sample.
options.rationale: A student who thinks one antibody binds a range of antigens picks this. It is wrong because an antibody that bound any antigen could not be used to measure the level of one particular hormone.

mcqs.stem: A patient with cancer is given a monoclonal antibody that has been bound to a toxic drug. The antibody binds to an antigen found on the patient's cancer cells. How does this treatment work?

options.text: It carries the toxic drug to every body cell.
options.rationale: A student who thinks a monoclonal antibody binds a range of antigens expects the drug to be spread everywhere. It is wrong because the antibody binds to one antigen, so the drug is delivered to the cancer cells without harming other cells in the body.

options.text: It stops the toxic drug causing side effects.
options.rationale: A student who believes monoclonal antibodies remove all side effects picks this. It is wrong because the antibody targets the drug rather than disarming it, and monoclonal antibodies create more side effects than expected.

options.text: It destroys the cancer cells as it binds to them.
options.rationale: A student who believes the antibody itself kills the cell it binds to picks this. It is wrong because the cancer cells are killed by the substance the antibody is bound to, which the antibody delivers to them.

options.text: It delivers the toxic drug to the cancer cells.
options.rationale: Correct. For cancer the monoclonal antibody can be bound to a toxic drug, and it delivers the substance to the cancer cells without harming other cells in the body.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about monoclonal antibodies is correct?

options.text: They create more side effects than expected.
options.rationale: Correct. Monoclonal antibodies create more side effects than expected, and they are not yet as widely used as everyone hoped when they were first developed.

options.text: They bind to several different protein antigens.
options.rationale: A student who thinks one antibody has a range of targets picks this. It is wrong because monoclonal antibodies are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen.

options.text: They create fewer side effects than expected.
options.rationale: A student who believes targeting removes side effects picks this. It is wrong because monoclonal antibodies create more side effects than expected, which is why they are not yet as widely used as everyone hoped.

options.text: They kill cancer cells with no substance bound.
options.rationale: A student who believes binding alone destroys the cell picks this. It is wrong because for cancer the antibody is bound to a radioactive substance, a toxic drug or a chemical which stops cells growing and dividing.
